title-group.article-title: Impact of semaglutide use on glycemic and metabolic profile in adults with type 1 diabetes having overweight or obesity: A systematic review and meta-analysis

sec.title: Background:
sec.p: Semaglutide is not yet approved for type 1 diabetes (T1D), but increasing evidence indicates it could offer clinical benefits for T1D patients, particularly those with overweight or obesity. Currently, no systematic review or meta-analysis has assessed semaglutide’s effectiveness in adults with T1D with overweight or obesity; this systematic review and meta-analysis aims to fill that knowledge gap.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: Electronic databases were searched for articles on semaglutide use in adults with T1D with overweight or obesity. Co-primary outcomes were the percent changes in body weight and glycated hemoglobin from baseline; secondary outcomes were changes in total daily dose of insulin, glycemic variability, and adverse events. Statistical analysis was performed with RStudio software (Posit Software, PBC, Boston ), and results are presented as mean differences (MDs) along with 95% confidence intervals.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Data from 8 studies involving adults with T1D having overweight/obesity (N = 274, with diabetes duration ranging from 19.7 to 33 years) were analyzed. All studies had a low risk of bias. Semaglutide use was associated with reductions in body weight from baseline at 3 months (MD −3.27% [−6.07 to −0.47]), 6 months (MD −6.53% [−8.44 to −4.63]), and 12 months (MD −7.6% [−8.16 to −7.04]). There was also a reduction in glycated hemoglobin from baseline at 3 months (MD −0.54% [−0.62 to −0.46]), 6 months (MD −0.55% [−0.71 to −0.40]), and 12 months (MD −0.6% [−0.72 to −0.48]). Three months (MD −0.05 units/kg/d [−0.06 to −0.03]) and 6 months (MD −0.07 units/kg/d [−0.13 to −0.01]) but not 12 months (MD −0.00 units/kg/d [−0.06 to 0.05]) of semaglutide therapy were associated with a reduction in total daily dose of insulin. Time in range (MD 4.62% [0.85 to 8.39]) and time above range (MD −8.97% [−16.41 to −1.53]) improved after 3 months of semaglutide use. Adverse event data were scarce and mostly gastrointestinal.

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: In adults with T1D having overweight or obesity, short-term semaglutide effectively promotes weight loss, improves glycemic control, and reduces insulin requirements. More long-term randomized controlled trials with a diverse group of participants are needed to incorporate semaglutide into the routine clinical management of these patients.
Keywords: glycemic variability, HbA1c, insulin requirement, semaglutide, type 1 diabetes, weight loss

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) results from an autoimmune process that destroys pancreatic beta cells, leading to insulin deficiency and requiring lifelong insulin treatment.[1] Patients and doctors often struggle to achieve adequate glycemic control, with fewer than 20% of patients with T1D reaching their glycemic targets.[2] The reasons are multifaceted, involving the need for a comprehensive understanding and self-management of complex insulin regimens, as well as more rigorous adherence to dietary and lifestyle factors compared to type 2 diabetes (T2D).[2] The worldwide rise in obesity affects both individuals with T2D and T1D equally, highlighting the widespread impact of the obesity pandemic. Obesity is linked to insulin resistance, which subsequently reduces the effectiveness of insulin therapy in T1D, something akin to “insulin resistance.” This can also be considered the coexistence of T2D in patients with T1D, hence referred to as “double diabetes.”[3] Weight loss in individuals with T1D who have obesity improves glycemic control, along with a reduction in total daily dose (TDD) of insulin requirement. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis (SR/MA) has shown that glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, such as liraglutide, are effective for weight loss, improving glycemic control, and reducing insulin requirements in patients with T1D who have obesity.[4]

Among all the GLP-1 receptor agonists available for clinical use, semaglutide demonstrates the best glycemic efficacy and weight loss properties, surpassing liraglutide, dulaglutide, lixisenatide, exenatide, and others.[5,6] Several studies have been published evaluating the use of semaglutide in T1D, particularly among individuals with associated obesity.[7,8] The literature review revealed that, to date, no SR/MA has been published evaluating the efficacy and safety of semaglutide use in T1D. Therefore, this SR/MA was conducted to address this knowledge gap.

sec.title: 2.1. Ethical compliance
sec.p: This SR/MA was conducted according to the procedures outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses checklist.[9,10] The SR/MA is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251036653), and the protocol summary can be accessed online.

sec.title: 2.2. Search strategy
sec.p: A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases and registries, including MEDLINE (via PubMed), Scopus, the Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov. This search spanned from the inception of each database to June 15, 2025. The search strategy employed combinations of key terms, including “semaglutide” and “type 1 diabetes.” The search terms were implemented in the titles and abstracts of the documents. The goal was to identify published and unpublished full-length journal articles and abstracts for the conference proceedings, all in English. Additionally, the search entailed examining references in the published articles obtained for this study and in relevant journals.

sec.title: 2.3. Eligibility criteria
sec.p: The PICOS criteria were utilized to screen and select the studies. The population (P) consisted of adults with overweight or obesity living with T1D. The intervention (I) consisted of using semaglutide in conjunction with standard-of-care insulin therapy for managing T1D. The control (C) group (if available) received either the standard-of-care insulin therapy alone or a placebo/any other approved medication in addition to the standard-of-care insulin therapy for T1D. In addition, studies without a control group were considered for single-arm and proportion meta-analysis. The outcomes (O) focused on percent weight reduction, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), total daily dose of insulin (TDDI) required, time in range (TIR; 70–180 mg/dL), time above range (TAR; >180 mg/dL), time below range (TBR; <70 mg/dL), and adverse events including hypoglycemia. The study type (S) included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, case-control studies, and case series. Cross-sectional studies, case reports, reviews, expert opinions, editorials, and letters to the editor were excluded from the analysis. Duplicates were removed before screening articles by title and abstract, followed by full-text screening to confirm eligibility.

sec.title: 2.4. Study selection
sec.p: Three reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the identified studies. They reviewed the full texts to determine if a study could not be excluded based solely on the title and abstract. Any disagreements regarding the study’s eligibility were resolved through consensus.

sec.title: 2.5. Study outcomes
sec.p: The primary outcomes examined were the changes from baseline in body weight (as a percent change) and HbA1c after 3, 6, and 12 months of semaglutide therapy, as measured at the end of the studies. Secondary outcomes included the percent change in TDDI requirement, TIR, TAR, TBR, and adverse events such as hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis after 3, 6, and 12 months of treatment with semaglutide.

sec.title: 2.6. Data extraction
sec.p: Two review authors independently extracted data using standardized data extraction forms. When multiple publications from a single study group were identified, the results were consolidated, and relevant data from each article were included in the analyses. The following data were extracted from all eligible studies and included in the review: first author, year of publication, the country where the study was conducted, study design, major inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size, proportions of female and male subjects, mean age, and body-weight body mass index of the participants, duration of T1D, HbA1c, TDD of insulin, proportions of study subjects using different insulin delivery methods, and the outcomes as mentioned above. Any disagreements were resolved by consensus.

sec.title: 2.7. Data synthesis and statistical analysis
sec.p: The extracted data were analyzed using the “meta” and “metafor” packages in RStudio for the R Statistics program (Version 2025.4.5.0).[11] The results were reported as mean differences (MDs) for continuous variables and risk ratios for categorical variables, each with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For studies involving a non-semaglutide control group, the MDs for changes from baseline values of the continuous outcomes in the semaglutide and control groups, as well as the risk ratio for the categorical variables, were calculated. For single-arm studies using only semaglutide, the mean changes from baseline values of the continuous outcomes were pooled to estimate effect sizes. The random-effects model was chosen to address the anticipated heterogeneity resulting from population characteristics in the included studies. The inverse variance statistical method was applied for all instances. Details of the meta-analysis included the use of the restricted maximum-likelihood estimator for tau², as well as the Q-profile method for the CIs of tau² and tau. Calculation of I2 was based on Q statistics using untransformed (raw) means. Forest plots were generated with the same software.

sec.title: 2.8. Assessment of the risk of bias in the included studies
sec.p: Two authors independently evaluated the risk of bias (RoB). The Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials version 2 (RoB2) was used to assess the RoB of RCTs, while the Risk of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions version 2 (ROBINS-I V2) was applied to non-randomized intervention trials and retrospective cohort studies.[12,13] RoB2 and ROBINS-I V2 assessments are described elsewhere.[14] In the event of disagreements, the sixth and seventh authors served as arbitrators to reach a consensus. The Risk-of-bias VISualization (robvis) web app was used to generate RoB plots.[15]

sec.title: 2.9. Assessment of heterogeneity
sec.p: The assessment of heterogeneity was initially performed by examining forest plots. Subsequently, Chi-square tests were conducted using N-1 degrees of freedom and a significance level of 0.05 to assess statistical significance. The I2 test was also used in the subsequent analysis. Thresholds for I² values were defined as 25% for low heterogeneity, 50% for moderate heterogeneity, and 75% for high heterogeneity.[16]

sec.title: 3.1. Search results and characteristics of the studies
sec.p: The initial search identified 254 articles. After removing 26 duplicates, 228 articles remained and were reviewed in detail. Figure 1 illustrates the study selection process. Nine articles were found on our topic of interest, of which 8 articles, including 274 patients with T1D and overweight or obesity who received standard care and were treated with semaglutide (fulfilling all the inclusion and exclusion criteria), were included in the analysis.[7,8,17–22] The study by Almohareb et al was excluded from analysis because it reported data from patients receiving semaglutide or liraglutide; outcomes from patients receiving only semaglutide were not available for analysis from that study.[23] The characteristics of the included and excluded studies in the SR/MA have been summarized in Table 1 and Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/Q860, respectively. Of the 8 included studies, 7 involved adults with overweight or obesity who have long-standing T1D (duration > 15 years) and a baseline HbA1c > 7%, which have been analyzed and presented in the forest plots. The majority of the study participants were women. Injectable once-weekly semaglutide was used in all the studies at doses ranging from 0.25 to 2 mg/wk. The results from the study by Dandona et al were not combined with others because the patients’ profiles were completely different. Dandona et al observed that in a cohort of young, normal body mass index adults with recent-onset T1D of <3 months, having a baseline HbA1c > 10%, the use of semaglutide with insulin over 1 year was linked to remission or the induction of the “honeymoon phase” in these individuals with T1D.[7]

sec.title: 3.2. Risk of bias and quality assessment of the included studies
sec.p: The overall risk of bias was low among the studies analyzed in this SR/MA. Details are provided in Figure S1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/Q860. Publication bias assessment was not performed due to the presence of fewer than 10 studies in the forest plots.[24]

sec.title: 3.3. Percent change in body weight from baseline
sec.p: Four studies with 147 patients, 7 studies with 224 patients, and 2 studies with 100 patients reported percent body weight reduction from baseline after 3, 6, and 12 months of semaglutide therapy, respectively. Three-month semaglutide therapy was associated with a 3.27% reduction (95% CI [−6.07 to −0.47], I2 = 92%) in body weight from baseline (Fig. 2A). Six-month semaglutide therapy resulted in a 6.53% reduction (95% CI [−8.44 to −4.63], I2 = 98.5%) in body weight from baseline (Fig. 2B). After 12 months, body weight reduced by 7.6% (95% CI [−8.16 to −7.04], I2 = 0%) from baseline (Fig. 2C).

caption.p: Forest plot showing the effect of semaglutide therapy in type 1 diabetes on percent weight reduction from baseline at 3 months (A), 6 months (B), and 12 months (C).

sec.title: 3.4. Change in HbA1c from baseline
sec.p: After 3 months of using semaglutide (in 4 studies; n = 160), HbA1c decreased by 0.54% (95% CI [−0.62 to −0.46], I2 = 89.3%) from baseline (Fig. 3A). The extent of HbA1c reduction at 6 months (in 4 studies; n = 148) and 12 months (in 2 studies; n = 100) was 0.55% (95% CI [−0.71 to −0.40], I2 = 97.4%; Fig. 3B), and 0.60% (95% CI [−0.72 to −0.48], I2 = 94.2%; Fig. 3C), respectively.

caption.p: Forest plot showing the effect of semaglutide therapy in type 1 diabetes on changes in glycated hemoglobin (%) from baseline at 3 months (A), 6 months (B), and 12 months (C).

sec.title: 3.5. TTDI requirement
sec.p: Three months of semaglutide use (in 4 studies; n = 135) resulted in a reduction in TDDI requirement from baseline by 0.05 units/kg/d (95% CI [−0.06 to −0.03], I2 = 87%; Fig. 4A). Such benefit was also observed at 6 months (in 4 studies; n = 147) with an MD of −0.07 units/kg/d (95% CI [−0.13 to −0.01], I2 = 96.5%; Fig. 4B). However, after 12 months (in 3 studies; n = 123), semaglutide was not associated with any reduction in TDD of insulin (MD −0.00 units/kg/d, 95% CI [−0.06 to 0.05], I2 = 98.5%; Fig. 4C).

caption.p: Forest plot showing the effect of semaglutide therapy in type 1 diabetes on changes in total daily dose of insulin (units/kg/d) from baseline at 3 months (A), 6 months (B), and 12 months (C).

sec.title: 3.6. TIR, TAR, and TBR
sec.p: After 3 months of using semaglutide (in 4 studies; n = 121), the percentage of time spent in TIR increased by 4.62% (95% CI [0.85 to 8.39], I2 = 99.6%) from baseline (Fig. 5A). The extent of TIR increment at 6 months (in 4 studies; n = 121) and 12 months (in 2 studies; n = 61) was 4.92% (95% CI [−0.60 to 10.44], I2 = 99.8%; Fig. 5B), and 2.73% (95% CI [−1.87 to 7.34], I2 = 98.9%; Fig. 5C), respectively. There was a reduction in TAR from baseline, as reported by 2 studies (n = 60) after 3 months (MD −8.97%, 95% CI [−16.41 to −1.53], I2 = 95.2%; Fig. 5D). After 3 months (in 2 studies; n = 60), a small increment in TBR (MD 0.30%, 95% CI [0.23 to 0.37], I2 = 0%) was also observed (Fig. 5E).

caption.p: Forest plot showing the effect of semaglutide therapy in type 1 diabetes on changes from baseline in time in range at 3 months (A), time in range at 6 months (B), time in range at 12 months (C), time above range at 3 months (D), and time below range at 3 months (E).

sec.title: 3.7. Adverse events
sec.p: Most studies had limited data on adverse events. Grassi et al noted that 4 of the 11 study participants (36.36%) had temporary nausea when starting or increasing semaglutide doses, with no reports of other side effects such as vomiting, constipation, or ketoacidosis.[20] Dandona et al observed mild hypoglycemia during dose escalation of semaglutide; however, no hypoglycemia was reported when patients were on stable doses of semaglutide.[7] Pasqua et al observed gastrointestinal side effects in 27% of patients. Two participants experienced euglycemic ketosis, which did not cause overt acidosis and was managed by increasing carbohydrate intake and insulin doses.[8] The most frequently reported adverse events in Shah et al study involved gastrointestinal symptoms. Both the semaglutide and placebo groups had 2 patients each experience severe hypoglycemia. Notably, 1 severe hypoglycemia event in the semaglutide group occurred 2 weeks after the trial ended, during the observation period, and another was caused by infusion-site failure.[22] None of these studies reported cases of diabetic ketoacidosis.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: Semaglutide has proven to be a powerful and effective treatment for obesity and T2D, offering positive effects on metabolic issues linked to steatotic liver disease, as well as improving cardiovascular and renal outcomes, all without elevating cancer risk.[25–27] Obesity has also become a significant issue among people living with T1D. Recent data indicate that 30%, 41%, and 62% of people with T1D in Europe, Brazil, and the USA, respectively, have overweight or obesity.[28–30] This is the first SR/MA to evaluate the impact of semaglutide use in individuals living with T1D on body weight, glycemic control, insulin requirements, and glycemic variability. Our analysis indicates that using semaglutide for 3 to 12 months in overweight to obese adults with T1D on standard insulin therapy can reduce body weight, HbA1c, and TDDI, while positively affecting TIR and TAR. Body weight reduction was evident at 3 months (MD −3.27%), persisted at 6 months (MD −6.53%), and was most pronounced at 12 months (−7.6%) after starting semaglutide use. Similarly, a sustained benefit of semaglutide in lowering HbA1c was also observed with both short-term (MD −0.54% after 3 months) and long-term use (MD −0.6% after 12 months). Since the TDDI requirement depends on an individual’s weight, notable weight loss with semaglutide use in T1D likely contributed to the reductions in insulin needs over 6 months (MD −0.07 units/kg/d) after starting the medication. Adding semaglutide additionally enhances glycemic variability, at least in the short term, as evidenced by notable improvements in TIR (MD 4.62%) and TAR (MD −8.97%) after 3 months of semaglutide initiation. However, the combination of semaglutide with insulin might raise the risk of hypoglycemia, which could explain the slight rise in TBR observed in this SR/MA. Semaglutide initiation in T1D should be closely monitored, with more intensive self-monitoring of blood glucose during the first few weeks and months, allowing for more effective insulin dose adjustments to prevent hypoglycemia and glycemic variability. The potential risk of euglycemic ketosis should also be considered.

In a systematic review of 5 RCTs (n = 2445), liraglutide 1.8 mg/d was associated with a mild HbA1c reduction (−0.24%) and a modest weight loss (−4.87 kg), along with a decrease in TDD of insulin requirements in patients with T1D.[31] Gastrointestinal problems were the primary side effects, with no increase in the risk of ketoacidosis.[31] Mild weight benefits have also been documented with the use of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors and metformin in people with T1D who have obesity.[32] In contrast, the reductions in weight, HbA1c, and TDD of insulin were much greater with semaglutide in our SR/MA. A recent SR/MA found that tirzepatide benefits adults with T1D and obesity by enhancing glycemic control (HbA1c reduction up to 0.78%), promoting weight loss (up to 15.70%), lowering TDDI (up to 36.19%), and reducing glycemic variability. These improvements observed at 6 months persisted and even continued to improve after 12 months of treatment.[33] Thus, the novel long-acting GLP-1 agonists and dual agonists offer metabolic benefits when used judiciously in adults with T1D and obesity.

The limitation of our SR/MA was that only single-arm (pre and posttreatment) SR/MA could be performed, as most studies on semaglutide in T1D lacked a valid matched control group. Additionally, the number of studies and the size of the studied populations were quite limited. All were single-center studies lacking global representation. All the studies included T1D adults with overweight or obesity; semaglutide has not been studied in lean T1D, and its use in such patients should be discouraged until we have good safety and efficacy data. All studies on T1D have used once-weekly injectable semaglutide; there is no data on the safety and effectiveness of oral semaglutide in T1D. Currently, there is no available data concerning the use of semaglutide in children and adolescents with T1D who also have obesity or metabolic syndrome. Moreover, evidence regarding the effectiveness of semaglutide in both normal-weight children and adults is missing. These topics warrant further research. Additionally, high heterogeneity was seen in most outcomes. Due to the small number of included studies and the nearly identical baseline characteristics, we were unable to perform subgroup analyses or sensitivity analyses to identify potential sources of heterogeneity.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: Semaglutide, when used alongside standard insulin therapy, effectively promotes weight loss and enhances glycemic control in adults with long-standing T1D who are overweight or obese. The positive effects observed at 3 months continued and even intensified after 12 months of treatment. Longer-term RCTs involving a diverse patient population are necessary to investigate the use of semaglutide in T1D.
